title: The AI Physician
answer: Ten areas where artificial intelligence is changing medicine: imaging, genomics, clinical documentation, surgery, intensive care, drug discovery, telemedicine, population health, the brain, and the regulation and security of the devices doing the work.

sections.body: This field is the application of artificial intelligence to medical practice, from reading scans to writing notes. AI is now doing concrete work in hospitals and labs: image classifiers flag possible fractures and bleeds in radiology, language models draft clinical notes from recorded visits, and molecular simulation screens compounds before wet lab testing. In surgery, navigation systems guide instruments using preoperative images, while intensive care units run predictive models for deterioration. The section covers ten areas where these tools are in active use, not just research.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Diagnostic imaging has the most mature and widely deployed models, with many cleared for clinical use, but they still miss rare findings and can be brittle on data from new scanners. Genomic and drug discovery tools accelerate candidate generation, yet most predictions fail in later trials. Clinical documentation is improving, but ambient systems still produce errors that require clinician review. Predictive analytics in intensive care can flag risk, but false alarms and workflow friction limit adoption. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models and 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows both the scale of activity and the real consequences of failure. Honest limits include narrow training data, unclear liability, and a shortage of prospective evidence.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader looking at how AI reads images would start with Diagnostic Imaging and Radiology, while Genomic Medicine and Precision Therapeutics covers the use of sequence and biomarker data to match treatments. Clinical Documentation and Ambient Intelligence explains the tools that listen to visits and draft notes, and Surgical Robotics and Navigation covers systems that assist in the operating room. Predictive Patient Analytics and Intensive Care is where early warning scores and deterioration models live, and Drug Discovery and Molecular Simulation follows the pipeline from target to candidate molecule. Telemedicine and Triage covers chatbots and remote assessment, Epidemiology and Population Health looks at outbreak tracking and risk stratification across groups, and Neuroinformatics and the Brain covers brain imaging and neural data. Governance, Compliance and Medical Device Security is the place for the rules, audits, and security problems that apply to all the others.
